cannot_tell.text: The lines rest on 11 US places that chose to zone a district near some of their stops, often on land builders already wanted. A state mandate makes every city act, on land it may pick less well, so it may do less. Near Milwaukee's new streetcar, building rose by a similar amount with no rezoning, so part of the measured gain may come from new transit or booming neighborhoods rather than zoning.
cannot_tell.title: Whether a required district does as well as a chosen one

cannot_tell.text: The places' districts averaged about 12% of the land within ¼ mile; the law asks for 15%. The central line does not scale it. Among the 11 places the effect fell as the district share grew, so scaling up (the former upper line, 12,521) leans on the smallest districts.
cannot_tell.title: Whether a bigger district adds proportionally more

cannot_tell.text: Stops on new lines gained about 18 extra homes per 100 lot acres a year with no rezoning (about 5,300 homes in Wisconsin over five years). That belongs to current law, not the law. Compared only with stops on lines of a similar age, the central falls to about 6,930. Massachusetts' district law shows no rise in its first year, and in Los Angeles a bigger density bonus at the tier lines did not add building.
cannot_tell.title: How much comes from the new lines themselves

cannot_tell.text: These results describe districts, not citywide upzoning. For the five broad upzonings left out (Bellevue's BelRed, Honolulu, Los Angeles, San Diego, Chicago 2022), the average rule missed by a median 43 extra homes per 100 lot acres a year, the scaled rule by 240, and simply predicting zero by 11. At their boundaries, too, these broad upzonings show no jump.
cannot_tell.title: Whether a citywide upzoning would do the same

cannot_tell.text: We tested 12 local traits (home values, incomes, rents, lot sizes, existing density, distance to downtown and others) and all 66 pairs of them, then 91 census variables (housing, incomes, commuting, car ownership and more), with 8 prediction methods including random and causal forests, predicting each of 8 cities from the others. None reliably predicts where upzoning added more homes, so the scenarios stay wide (docs/tod/TRAITS_RESULTS.md, docs/tod/ALLVARS_RESULTS.md).
cannot_tell.title: Why the response differs from place to place

cannot_tell.text: The places' effects were measured over the years after each reform. The model places that effect inside 2027–2031, the law's first five years. Much of a real law's effect may come after 2031, so the yearly path is the least certain part of these numbers.
cannot_tell.title: Timing

cannot_tell.text: The tool has no case in which the extra homes near stops are simply moved from elsewhere in the same city. Whole-city permit counts could only detect a change of about 4% to 5% of a city's homes over five years, so they cannot rule a small shift in or out. At district edges, the lots just outside showed no drop in building (the bunching check), which is where a shift would show first.
cannot_tell.title: Homes that would have been built elsewhere in the city anyway

cannot_tell.text: The cases cannot separate the two. The parking reform has its own scenario in this tool.
cannot_tell.title: Transit-oriented density alone versus with parking reform

cannot_tell.text: The model works by place. Nothing here says what will be built on any one lot.
cannot_tell.title: Lot-by-lot predictions

rows.text: Stacy and others (2023): about +0.8% more addresses after a loosening reform in 1,136 US cities. Most of those reforms were about accessory dwellings and lot sizes, not transit.

trace.text: Stop locations from the federal National Transit Map; frequencies from each agency's own schedule file or, for Madison, its published route descriptions.

Each place's expected new homes under current law (Census building permits, 2023–2025 average, with Milwaukee's apartments counted from its property records), times its share of homes near stops.

All three lines come from our own lot-by-lot data on US places that zoned a district for denser housing near some of their rail or rapid stops (docs/tod/CAUSAL_FRAMEWORK_PLAN.md, docs/tod/OPTION_D_PLAN.md). Central: the 11 places' average effect within ¼ mile, against similar stops without reform (no model beat this average on places it had not seen). Lower: the edge test, inside versus just outside district boundaries in 5 places: the rezoned lots' own gain only. Upper: rezoned stops on new lines against new-line stops not rezoned. Land beyond ¼ mile counts zero. Earlier lines are shown as comparisons.

trace.part: That those results carry over to Wisconsin
trace.text: No Wisconsin outcome has tested the sizing. The training cities chose their district land, often land builders already wanted; Wisconsin's district is modelled as spread at random over the ¼-mile land, and a mandate may do less than a city's own choice. A check near Milwaukee's streetcar, with no rezoning, found building rose about as much as in a typical reform place, so quarter-mile gains of that size can happen without zoning changes.
All three lines follow the build-up measured after the New York rezonings.

The district is spread at random over the land within ¼ mile of rail and rapid stops, so each place gets the statewide homes in proportion to its lot acres there. Milwaukee and Madison get 82% of the central line's homes; suburbs with rail or rapid stops (Wauwatosa, Kenosha, Shorewood Hills, Sun Prairie and others) get the rest.
Each place's numbers are split across districts in proportion to where its detached houses are (the same split the ADU screens use), not by homes near stops.
